question:
A 27-year-old man comes to the physician because of worsening abdominal pain over the last several months. He has also had recent feelings of sadness and a lack of motivation at work, where he is employed as a computer programmer. He denies suicidal thoughts. He has a history of multiple kidney stones. He has a family history of thyroid cancer in his father and uncle, who both underwent thyroidectomy before age 30. His temperature is 37°C (98°F), blood pressure is 138/86 mm Hg, and pulse is 87/min. Physical examination shows diffuse tenderness over the abdomen and obesity but is otherwise unremarkable. Serum studies show:
Na+ 141 mEq/L
K+ 3.6 mEq/L
Glucose 144 mg/dL
Ca2+ 12.1 mg/dL
Albumin 4.1 g/dL
PTH 226 pg/mL (normal range 12–88 pg/mL)
Results of a RET gene test return abnormal. The physician refers him to an endocrine surgeon. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?"?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: RET gene test abnormal -> Suspected multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndrome -> Possible MEN type 2 -> 80% CHAIN: High PTH level -> Hyperparathyroidism -> Possible primary hyperparathyroidism -> 75% CHAIN: Abdominal pain and kidney stones -> Hypercalcemia -> Possible primary hyperparathyroidism -> 70% CHAIN: Family history of thyroid cancer -> Increased risk for medullary thyroid carcinoma -> Possible MEN type 2 -> 80%
analysis: The patient presents with symptoms of abdominal pain, sadness, lack of motivation, and a family history of thyroid cancer. The elevated calcium levels and high PTH levels suggest primary hyperparathyroidism. Given the abnormal RET gene test and the need for referral to an endocrine surgeon, the most appropriate next step in diagnosis would be thyroidectomy to address the potential presence of a medullary thyroid carcinoma associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) syndrome.
